new_statements.quote: Both kʸílp- and kʸálp derive from earlier *kʸélp, which is in turn analyzable into a prefix kʸə- and a root lVp, probably *lep; stress usually falls on the root in present-day Nisgha, but there is evidence that stress often fell on prefixes at an earlier stage of the language. [fn 11, p. 81:] Since -o:l carries the stress in all cases, it is unlikely that it is a true suffix, as the overwhelming majority of true suffixes are unstressed. [fn 18, p. 82:] the suffix -l, like most Nisgha suffixes, never changes the stress pattern of a word
new_statements.citation: Tarpent, Marie-Lucie. 1983. The evolution of the Nisgha counting system: a window on cultural change. Working Papers of the Linguistics Circle of the University of Victoria 3(1): 60-86.
new_statements.locator: pp. 66-67 (section 2.3 'Two'); see also fn 11 p. 81 and fn 18 p. 82
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (27-page scan with text layer; title page p. 60: "The Evolution of the Nisgha Counting System: A Window on Cultural Change, Marie-Lucie Tarpent, University of Victoria"). Rendered PDF pages 7-8 (printed pp. 66-67, section 2.3 'Two') at 100 dpi and read the page images: p. 66 ends "..analyzable into a prefix k(y)ə- and a root lVp, probably *lep; stress usually falls on the" and p. 67 begins "root in present-day Nisgha, but there is evidence that stress often fell on prefixes at an earlier stage of the language." The English is verbatim; the reader's kʸ transliteration of Tarpent's k-with-superscript-y is a rendering choice only. Text layer also confirms fn 11 (block followed by page n…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is assigned morphologically: it falls on the (monosyllabic, typically CVC) root; proclitics and prefixes preceding the root and the suffixes following it are unstressed and do not shift stress. Tarpent's plural paper (KWPL 1983, pp. 163-165) confirms this: proclitics 'are never stressed', and a handful of plurals with stress on the prefix are 'an exception.. to the great majority of Nisgha words', relics of an earlier initial-stress stage. Compare Gitksan (Brown et al. 2016, after Rigsby 1986): stress on the rightmost vowel of the root, suffixes invisible.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: A few words carry stress on a prefix rather than the root (KWPL 1983 pp. 164-165: límqs 'to grow (pl.)', lískʸit 'to be born (pl.)', and the numeral txálpx where the proclitic txa- 'all' carries stress, WPLC 1983 p. 70); some stressed suffix-like elements such as -o:l in the 'persons' numerals are argued to be former nouns/compound members rather than true suffixes (fn 11). Diachronically Tarpent reconstructs initial (or penultimate) stress for the earliest stage and a later shift 'to the second or last syllable' (KWPL 1983 pp. 194-195).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root + affixes/proclitics); no phrase-level or citation-form discussion. The statement is a passing remark in an etymological paper by the language's principal grammarian, not a phonology section, hence medium confidence; Tarpent's 900-page grammar (1989) would supersede it.
new_statements.identity_note: All Tarpent sources describe Nisga'a (Nisgha/Nishga) of the Nass River, glottocode nisg1240, from her own fieldwork; Boas 1911 describes the same 'Nass' dialect. The Brown et al. 2016 JIPA illustration saved in the folder is Gitksan (gitx1241), the sister variety of the Nass-Gitksan continuum, and is NOT the basis of the statement.

new_statements.quote: Nass-Gitksan is actually a very analytic language. Affixes are few in number; they are mostly suffixes. For the naive listener, an illusion of synthesis results from the stress pattern in Nass-Gitksan. Only heads of phrases and the second members of compounds receive primary stress. All other adverbial and adnominal elements are proclitic and unstressed.
new_statements.citation: Rigsby, Bruce. 1967. Tsimshian comparative vocabularies with notes on Nass-Gitksan systematic phonology. Proceedings of the 2nd International Conference on Salish (and Neighboring) Languages, 1-41.
new_statements.locator: p. 21 (PDF p. 24), end of the phonology notes, just before the asterisk rule; verified against the page image. See also p. 14 (PDF p. 17) and p. 16 (PDF p. 19) for 'final stressed syllables'.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opens (41 pp., text layer). The quote is verbatim on printed p. 21 = PDF p. 24, last paragraph before the asterisk line, checked on the page image: 'Nass-Gitksan is actually a very analytic language. Affixes are few in number; they are mostly suffixes. For the naive listener, an illusion of synthesis results from the stress pattern in Nass-Gitksan. Only heads of phrases and the second members of compounds receive primary stress. All other adverbial and adnominal elements are proclitic and unstressed.' The 'short final stressed syllables' (p. 14 = PDF p. 17) and 'final stressed open syllables' (p. 16 = PDF p. 19) references are also there. No word-stress placement rule anywhere in the n…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's root-stress statement (proclitics/adverbial and adnominal elements are unstressed; the head/lexical element carries primary stress) and adds the compound rule (second member stressed) and the phrasal domain. It does not itself say stress is on the root. NB the work treats Nass (Nisgha) and Gitksan as one language, 'Nass-Gitksan', and the cover letter says cited forms are Gitksan unless indicated.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress placement within a word. The one general statement is at phrase/compound level: only heads of phrases and second members of compounds receive primary stress; all other adverbial and adnominal elements are proclitic and unstressed. Phonological rules elsewhere refer to 'short final stressed syllables' (spirant lengthening, p. 14; h-offglide after short vowels 'in final stressed open syllables', p. 16), which presupposes that stress commonly sits on a word-final syllable, but this is never stated as a rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Rigsby 1967 treats Nass (Nisgha) and Gitksan as a single language, 'Nass-Gitksan', distinct from Coast Tsimshian, and its cover letter says cited forms are Gitksan unless indicated, so its phrase-stress statement is for Nass-Gitksan as a whole. Tarpent 1994 covers all Tsimshianic languages; 'N' forms are Nisgha and the synchronic rule is stated for the present languages generally, with Interior Tsimshianic (Nisgha and Gitksan) singled out as having adopted the root/final pattern earliest. Tarpent 1987 is Nisgha proper (School District 92, Nass Valley).

new_statements.quote: In the Tsimshianic languages, stress is usually on the root, which generally falls on the last syllable of the word, but a number of exceptions point to an earlier pattern of stress on the penultimate syllable, regardless of its morphological status. [...] It can also be shown that the penultimate stress-rule survived longer as a productive process in Maritime Tsimshianic (MT--Coast and Southern Tsimshian) than in Interior Tsimshianic (IT--Nisgha and Gitksan). [p. 243, sec. 1.1.2:] In the present languages, stress is usually on the root, or on a stressed suffix. [p. 257, sec. 1.5:] the more modern pattern places it preferably on the last syllable, usually the root.
new_statements.citation: Tarpent, Marie-Lucie. 1994. Tsimshianic stress assignment and the words for 'meat, bear'. Papers for the 29th ICSNL, pp. 243-262. (NOT among the listed works; found on the same lingpapers index page and downloaded because it is a stress paper.)
new_statements.locator: Abstract p. 243 and sec. 1.1.2 p. 243 (PDF p. 1); sec. 1.3.1 (compounds: 'In most compounds primary stress falls on the second element'); sec. 1.5 'General conclusion on stress patterns' p. 257 (PDF p. 8); sec. 2.1 p. 258: 'In the N and G words, stress occurs on the final syllable'; all verified against page images
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opens (11 pp., 2-up, scanned layer with w->y, g->. artifacts). Checked on page images of PDF pp. 1 and 8: abstract p. 243 reads exactly 'In the Tsimshianic languages, stress is usually on the root, which generally falls on the last syllable of the word, but a number of exceptions point to an earlier pattern of stress on the penultimate syllable, regardless of its morphological status.' and 'It can also be shown that the penultimate stress-rule survived longer as a productive process in Maritime Tsimshianic (MT--Coast and Southern Tsimshian) than in Interior Tsimshianic (IT--Nisgha and Gitksan).' Sentence 'In the present languages, stress is usually on the root, or on a stressed suffix.…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement from Tarpent 1983 (stress usually on the root; prefixes stressed at an earlier stage) and adds that the root is generally the word-final syllable, that some suffixes are stressed, that compounds stress the second element, and that the exceptions reflect an older penultimate rule. It also matches the Gitksan comparison (Brown et al. 2016: rightmost vowel of the root).
new_statements.rule_in_words: In present-day Nisgha (and the other Tsimshianic languages) stress is usually on the root, which generally is the last syllable of the word, or on a stressed suffix (e.g. detransitive -isT); in most compounds primary stress falls on the second lexical element. A residue of irregular forms (prefixed chiefly names, some plurals, old compounds) preserves an older pattern of stress on the penultimate syllable regardless of morphology; that archaic pattern died out earlier in Interior Tsimshianic (Nisgha, Gitksan) than in Coast/Southern Tsimshian.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such; sec. 1.3.1 notes the first (unstressed) element of a compound may be weakened.
new_statements.exceptions: Archaic penultimate stress in prefixed chiefly names ('Grandfather of..' prefix, sec. 1.1.2), some prefixed and reduplicated plurals (secs. 1.2.1.2, 1.2.2.1.2), and old compounds (sec. 1.3.2); stressed suffixes such as detransitive -isT (ex. 4, fn. 3); a few IT final-stress vs MT penultimate-stress correspondences (sec. 2).
new_statements.identity_note: Rigsby 1967 treats Nass (Nisgha) and Gitksan as a single language, 'Nass-Gitksan', distinct from Coast Tsimshian, and its cover letter says cited forms are Gitksan unless indicated, so its phrase-stress statement is for Nass-Gitksan as a whole. Tarpent 1994 covers all Tsimshianic languages; 'N' forms are Nisgha and the synchronic rule is stated for the present languages generally, with Interior Tsimshianic (Nisgha and Gitksan) singled out as having adopted the root/final pattern earliest. Tarpent 1987 is Nisgha proper (School District 92, Nass Valley).
